## Borrow Hindsight

A question to borrow from your future self: "How would I respond to this once I understood it more clearly, in balance and with compassion?" It can change how the whole thing looks. It can also just make you feel a bit more like that person, or less alone (sometimes all at once). Keep in mind it's only their best guess. No perfect Higher Self is handing down answers.

t65s_secsp5p2b:
## “And So That’s the Way It Happened!”

When a hard memory comes up and you can handle it, tell it to yourself like a story and finish with "And so that's the way it happened!" (If the start is the hard part, "Once upon a time…" gets you going.) It's a little corny, but the memory starts sounding like a chapter of your life, where before it sounded like a trial still in session, with you in the defendant's chair.

The story version is still true, and it's no proof you got every detail right. Listen to how the narrator sounds. A sneer means stop. So does more shame, or a feeling that you're not quite real, and stepping further back won't fix either one. If the line helps, leave it at one line (no epilogue needed).

t65s_sp9a2: Give every session with your little one a clear ending. Look around and say where you are. Feel your feet on the floor, or the chair under you, and let your jaw and hands go loose. Then name the next everyday thing you're about to do (answer that text, start the dishes) and say: "That's enough for today. We're going back to the life we're building." The feelings can stay a bit unsettled while you go make dinner.
t65s_sp9b2: Sessions need an ending, or they turn into the whole day. When you're done, look around and name the room you're in. Notice your feet, or the chair. Unclench your jaw and your hands (they're usually clenched). Pick the next everyday thing, like a shower, and say: "That's enough for today. We're going back to the life we're building." Then go do it, with whatever's still unsettled coming along.
t65s_sp9c2: End each session on purpose. Name where you are, out loud if nobody's around. Feel your feet or the chair, and let your jaw and hands relax. Then name what's next, like lunch, and tell your little one, "That's enough for today. We're going back to the life we're building." You don't need every feeling sorted out first, and lunch won't mind either way.

t65s_sp8p1a: When picturing your little one feels fake, try a photo instead. You don't have to make up their face or how they're standing (or the haircut), because it's all right there. Look at it gently and notice what comes up, without deciding first what the picture is supposed to prove.
t65s_sp8p1b: A real photo of you as a child can help when imagining one feels fake. Nobody has to invent a face or a posture; there you are, in that sweater. Look at it gently and see what comes up, and try not to decide ahead of time what it's supposed to prove.
t65s_sp8p1c: If you can't picture your little one without it feeling made up, dig out an actual photo. Then there's no face or posture to invent (it's all there, bangs and everything). Look at it gently and let whatever comes up come up, without deciding what the photo has to prove.
t65s_sp8p2a: While you look, notice what your body does, and what you feel or want to do, and what that younger you seems to want you to understand. Then sort it into piles, like laundry. What do you remember yourself, and what did someone tell you later? What are you guessing from the picture? And what might be an image, a dream or a metaphor, or just not knowing?
t65s_sp8p2b: While you look, notice what your body does and what feelings or urges show up, and what that younger you seems to want you to get. Then sort it. Some of it you'll remember yourself, and some of it someone told you later ("You hated that coat"). Some you're guessing from the picture. Some might be an image or a dream or a metaphor, or you honestly don't know.
t65s_sp8p3a: Some questions to skip: "What abuse must have happened?" "Who did this to me?" "What memory is my body hiding?" And don't keep questioning one photo until a story finally shows up. That's a real risk. Guided imagery and suggestive statements can create false memories, and [in one experiment](https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/BF03196318), half the people shown a doctored childhood photo came to remember, at least partly, a hot-air balloon ride they never took.
t65s_sp8p3b: Skip questions like "What abuse must have happened?", "Who did this to me?" or "What memory is my body hiding?" And if you catch yourself grilling the same photo until a story turns up, stop there. Suggestive questions and guided imagery can plant memories of things that never happened. [In one study](https://link.springer.com/article/10.3758/BF03196318), researchers put people's childhood photos into a hot-air balloon ride that never happened, and half of them came to remember it, at least partly.
t65s_sp8p4a: A photo is one moment that someone picked and framed. It doesn't show what was going on outside the frame, or why you looked the way you did that day. So it's like those hard dreams and session images: it can tell you something true about how you feel now without proving that its story happened. The same goes for a body reaction.
t65s_sp8p4b: Remember that somebody chose that moment and framed it. Whatever was happening outside the frame isn't in it, and neither is the reason you looked the way you did. A photo or a jolt in your body can say something real about how you feel today, the way a dream can, and still prove nothing about what happened back then.
t65s_sp8p5a: If something serious starts to take shape, like an accusation, don't confront anyone over what came up here alone. Write down exactly what came up and how, and take it to someone grounded who won't steer you toward the answer they'd like. Put the photo away when you're done, too. If it has you searching and needing to be sure, or it gets you dysregulated, set it aside for now and come back to calming down in the present.
t65s_sp8p5b: If it starts to look like something serious happened, don't confront or accuse anybody based only on what came up here. Write down what came up and how it came up. Then talk it over with someone steady who won't lead you toward an answer. And when you're done, put the photo away. If it keeps pulling you back to search it, or to be certain, stop using it for a while and get yourself regulated in the present first.
t65s_sp6p1f: When you wake up, pick one hook to watch for. Something like "Today I'll notice one hook before I act on it" is plenty (it's kind of a big ask anyway). At night, look back at the day the way you'd look over a friend's shoulder at theirs, kindly. Where did you notice the hook, and where did it run its whole routine anyway? What's the next small repair, or the next thing that would protect your little one?
t65s_sp6p1h: Mornings: one modest intention, and that's it. "Today I'll notice one hook before I act on it." Nights: a look back at the day, no grades given. Where did you notice the hook? And where did it go ahead and run the whole show anyway? Think about what small repair or protective thing comes next, too.
t65s_sp6p2h: And what good did you get today? Count the small stuff, like a warm moment, or some nerve you didn't know you had. Noticing the hook counts too, and it counts when you only caught it with half the text already written. Same if you broke the pattern somewhere. Then repair what you can, and that's the day. Same intention tomorrow. Bed.
t65s_sp6p2i: Look for the good stuff before you're done, a bit of warmth you got or a moment you were braver than usual. If you caught the hook, that's progress, embarrassingly late or not. If you interrupted the pattern, give that a nod too. Fix what's fixable. Then pick the same intention for tomorrow and go to sleep, because the review's over.
